description: Hi! We are an enthusiastic team ready to explore the next frontier in the Space Apps Challenge. We love space, science, and learning new things. Currently, we are looking for members with skills in programming/coding, graphic design, or data analysis to build an interactive solution together. Let's collaborate and solve real-world problems.
summary:
Lost & Found: Space Edition is a short animated film that turns NASA’s discarded hardware on the Moon and Mars into a story young space fans can actually follow. A child astronaut guides viewers across the lunar surface and the Martian plains, stopping at the landers, rovers and equipment humanity left behind — what each machine was sent to do, what it discovered, and why it stayed.

We chose storytelling over a database because the challenge targets school-age audiences. A 55-second animated narrative with a relatable guide holds a child’s attention in a way a catalogue of mission records cannot, and it travels easily through classrooms and social feeds.

This matters because these objects are usually dismissed as space junk. They are the physical record of how humanity learned to land, drive, dig and survive on other worlds — the first archaeology beyond Earth. Our film reframes them as monuments worth remembering, and asks the next generation what they would leave behind.
details:
What it does

Lost & Found: Space Edition is a 55-second animated film for school-age audiences about the hardware NASA has left behind on the Moon and Mars. Rather than presenting a catalogue of discarded equipment, it follows a young astronaut explorer who treats the surface of each world as a lost-and-found counter: every object she finds has an owner, a job it once did, and a discovery attached to it.

How it works

The film is built as a guided tour with three movements. It opens on the lunar surface, where descent stages, rovers and experiment packages sit where their missions ended. It then travels to Mars, where landers, rovers and entry hardware rest among the rocks. It closes by reframing the whole collection — not as junk, but as the record of everything humanity has learned about reaching another world. The child-guide narration keeps the register age-appropriate: short sentences, concrete questions, no jargon.

Tools used

The visuals were produced with [name your AI video generator — e.g. Veo / Sora / Runway / Kling], assembled and timed in [your editor — e.g. CapCut / Premiere / DaVinci Resolve], with narration and sound by [voice tool or recorded voice]. Frame interpolation to 60 fps and the on-screen “AI generated” label were applied with FFmpeg. Reference material for the hardware and its locations came from [NASA History Office catalogue of man-made material on the Moon / NASA Image and Video Library / NSSDCA — list what you actually used].

Benefits and goals

Most children encounter abandoned spacecraft, if at all, as the punchline of a “space junk” headline. This project aims to replace that framing with curiosity. A short, visual, shareable film fits where children already are — classroom projectors, phones, social feeds — and needs no app install, no hardware, and no reading level barrier. Our hope is that a child who watches it comes away able to name one machine left on another world and say what it found, and then asks the question the film ends on: what would you leave behind?
